issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may reject concurrent factual findings when the lower courts omitted material evidence that supports a contrary inference.
material_facts: The lower courts found that the tenants had constructed the balcony without the landlord’s consent.

They did not consider the omission of the balcony from two notices, the predecessor landlord’s testimony that he had not objected after the tenants promised to remove it, or his payment for a window that supplied light and air to it.
The courts relied on inferences about how the structure was fixed without supporting evidence.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were not binding because the lower courts had omitted material evidence and drawn inferences without considering evidence that could support a contrary conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, factual findings are not binding on the Supreme Court when the courts below omit material evidence and draw inferences without considering evidence that could support a contrary inference.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party brought an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging factual findings made by lower courts.
predicates.lower_courts_omitted_material_evidence: The lower courts did not consider evidence material to the factual conclusion they reached.
predicates.evidence_supported_contrary_inference: The omitted evidence supported an inference contrary to the one drawn by the lower courts.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court appeal challenges factual findings, omitted material evidence supporting a contrary inference means those findings are not binding.

issues.legal_issue: A removable wooden structure that does not substantially change a building’s form, character, front, or structure is not a material alteration supporting eviction on that ground.
material_facts: The structure was a wooden cabin and balcony inside a showroom, made of beams and planks with a wooden staircase.
The evidence did not establish that it was fixed to the walls or floor in a way that made it a substantial or damaging structural change.
The structure was removable, and the asserted ground for eviction was that it constituted a material alteration.
issues.conclusion: The wooden balcony did not amount to a material alteration that could support eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(c) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 requires a construction that materially alters the premises or is likely to diminish their value. Applying Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, the court considers the nature, character, extent, and permanence of the construction and whether it substantially changes the form, front, or structure of the premises; a temporary construction that can be removed without damage is relevantly different from a substantial structural change. Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das confirms that the assessment depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The provision does not require proof of diminished value in addition to material alteration.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and construction_is_removable and not substantial_change_to_building_structure

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the tenant made a material alteration to the premises.
predicates.construction_is_removable: The construction could be removed without causing substantial damage to the building.
predicates.substantial_change_to_building_structure: The construction substantially changed the form, front, character, or structure of the building.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction proceeding, a removable construction that does not substantially change the building’s structure is not a material alteration.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s conduct and the surrounding evidence may establish that a tenant’s construction was made with implied consent, or that the landlord gave up the objection to it.
material_facts: The predecessor landlord omitted the balcony from two notices sent before the eviction suit, despite its presence at the premises.
He testified that he had not objected after the tenants said they would remove the balcony when they vacated.
He paid for a window that provided light and air to the balcony.
The later purchasers continued the pending eviction suit.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not support a finding that the tenants had constructed the balcony without the landlord’s express or implied consent; the circumstances supported implied consent or, alternatively, waiver of the objection.
issues.legal_principle: The court inferred implied consent from the landlord’s conduct and the surrounding evidence. It also observed, relying on Dawsons Bank Ltd. v. Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha, that waiver is an agreement to release or not assert a right, but stated that it was unnecessary to discuss waiver further once the evidence did not establish construction without consent.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground of an unauthorized construction.
predicates.landlord_omitted_construction_from_notic: The landlord sent pre-suit notices while the construction was present but did not identify it as an objection or ground for eviction.
predicates.landlord_accepted_tenant_removal_assuran: The landlord refrained from objecting after the tenant said the construction would be removed when the tenant left.
predicates.landlord_paid_for_feature_serving_constr: The landlord paid for a feature that supplied light or air to the construction.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction proceeding, omission of the construction from notices, acceptance of an assurance that it would be removed, and payment for a feature serving it mean the construction is not established as having been made without the landlord’s consent.
